narration:
The organiser is a broad, grey-stubbled man with ink on his thumbs. He's pinning a fresh sheet over an old one (*Drover seeks guide, Marrow Fen road, fog season, pay on arrival*) when you suggest a game to pass the time. He laughs through the tacks in his mouth.

"Dice, is it?" He spits the tacks into his palm and looks you over properly: travel dust, worn boots, empty hands. "Corwin Hale. I run this board, and I've watched a fair few wanderers come through offering me a friendly game while I work."

He takes a pair of yellowed bone dice from his waistcoat pocket and rolls them across the top of the water trough. They come up a two and a five. "Mine. Been in my pocket eleven years. If we play, we play with these, on this trough, where I can see your hands." His smile stays friendly, but his eyes don't. "And a game needs a stake. Twelve silver, you said? Let's see yours on the stone first."

You go through your pockets and come up with one thing: your compass. There's no coin, and no loaded die either. Whatever you were going to palm, you aren't carrying it.

Corwin waits with the bone dice resting in his open hand and the half-pinned notice flapping behind him.

input: I tell the work organiser that a hero like me doesn't fill in notices: give me the best-paid job and its pay up front, free, now.

result.summary: 5 minutes pass (Talking with Tamsin Vey at the notice board)

narration:
The organiser doesn't look up from her ledger right away. She's a broad, weathered woman in a waxed coat, with a stub of charcoal behind one ear and a lantern hooked to the post beside the board. She finishes the line she's writing, blows on it, and only then looks you over: the road dust, the compass, the empty hands.

"Hero," she says, as if it's a word on a list of goods she doesn't stock. "Name's Tamsin Vey. I've been placing hands at this crossing for nineteen years. Pay up front, free, now? I'd be paying you to walk off down the road, and plenty have done exactly that."

She taps the board with the charcoal. Notices are pinned under it in rows: *Fence-mending, Orrin's lower field, 2 silver.* *Lost goats, ask at the tannery, 1 silver a head.* At the top, on newer paper, is one that pays more than the rest put together:

***GUIDE WANTED. Salt carts across the Greyling Fen to Hollow Ford. 12 silver, paid at the far side by the carters' master.***

"That's your best-paid job. It pays well because the last guide put two carts in the mire, and the road markers have sunk since the spring floods." Her eyes go back to the compass. "If you can actually read that thing, you might be worth it. The coin comes when the salt reaches Hollow Ford, not before. That isn't my rule. The carters won't pay a stranger for nothing, and neither will I."

She shuts the ledger with her thumb still in it. "If you want something tonight, I can stand you a meal and a cot at the carters' yard against your first pay. Leave a name I can write down and something I can hold till you're back. Otherwise the board's free to read and the road's free to walk."

narration:
The porter is easy to spot: a thick-necked young man with a coil of rope over one shoulder, sitting on an upturned salt crate by the board. He's been telling the lantern-light that nobody at this crossing can put his shoulders in the dust. When you step up, he looks you over the way Tamsin did, taking in the road dust and the empty hands, and grins.

"A taker." He stands. He's a head shorter than you and half again as wide. "Name's Bram. Three falls, shoulders down, no gouging. Loser stands the winner a cup at the yard." He spits in his palms. "You've got coin for a cup, have you?"

A few carters drift over from the yard gate. Tamsin doesn't move from the board, but her thumb stays in the ledger and her eyes don't leave you.

Bram comes in low, hands wide, the way men who carry salt sacks all day do.

narration:
Tamsin Vey hears you out, then finishes the line she was writing. She doesn't look up until she's blown the charcoal dry.

"The board hasn't got a key," she says. "It's nailed to the post. Anyone can read it. That's what a board is for." She slides the ledger under her arm, thumb still holding her page. "And my purse stays on my belt, where it's been for nineteen years. Plenty of men have told me what I'll do. I'm still waiting on the first one to be right."

She doesn't raise her voice. She doesn't need to. The carters who drifted over for the wrestling haven't gone back to the yard gate. One of them sets down the bucket he was carrying. Bram is still rubbing dust off his elbow from putting you down twice. He stops grinning and watches you the way he watched your feet before the first fall.

"Here's how it stands," Tamsin says. "A man who gets thrown and laughs it off, I can work with. A man who gets thrown and then tries to rob the woman holding the ledger, I can't put on a cart." She looks at the compass again, longer this time. "The offer stays open till the lantern's out. A name, something I can hold, and you guide the salt. Or the road's still free."

The carters wait to see which way you'll go.

narration:
The organiser is a broad, weathered man with a wax tablet hanging from his belt on a cord. He taps the board with a stub of stylus before you finish asking.

"Best pay? That one." He points to a sheet nailed higher than the rest. The ink has run a little, as if it got wet. "Twelve silver. Edda Marsh posted it. She's the toll warden down at Harrow Ford, an hour south along the cart road. The spring flood moved the river. The old ford's gone soft, and two carts have lost wheels in it this month. She wants somebody to find a new crossing through the reed flats, a safe one, and mark it with stakes so the carters can follow it."

He looks you over: the dust on your boots, the compass at your belt. "Most folk who come asking can't tell north in a fog. Twelve's a lot because nobody's taken it. The flats eat boots, and sometimes worse. And I'll say this before Edda does: Old Osric runs a ferry boat just upriver. He hasn't complained about the ford going bad. Not once."

He shrugs and moves his finger down the board. "The rest is plain stuff. Unloading grain at the granary pays three silver a day, more if your back holds up. Widow Pell's goat is loose somewhere, and that's one silver if you find it alive." He taps the tablet. "I take one coin in ten for the matching. Name's Tobin Vell. And yours, if you're putting it down for anything?"

narration:
Tobin's stylus stops halfway down the board. He follows your gaze to the sheets, then looks back at you, one eyebrow up.

"Flour job?" He taps each notice in turn, the way he'd count coins. "Ford crossing, twelve silver. Granary, three a day. Pell's goat, one silver. That's the lot." He leans in and squints at the board, as if a fourth sheet might have grown there while he wasn't watching. "No bakery on here. Haven't been sacks to hand out since harvest. And I don't keep stock. I match folk to work, I don't carry the work around in my pockets."

He doesn't sound angry, just careful. He's a man who has been sweet-talked out of a tenth before.

"If it's sacks you want, the granary's the nearest thing to it. Out past the well, the big barn with the green doors. Old Haskett runs the unloading, three silver for a full day, and he pays at sundown, not before. I'll put your mark down for it if you like." He lifts the wax tablet on its cord and holds the stylus over it. "But I'll need a name to put it against. Or at least a mark I'll know again."

Behind him a cart rattles into the square loaded with empty barrels. The driver waves at Tobin, and Tobin lifts two fingers back without looking away from you.

narration:
You reach for your belt, and your hand finds only the compass. There's no receipt to show because no sacks ever left this square. There's no ledger either. You haven't walked the north road yet, and its ditches are still out there ahead of you.

Tobin watches your hand come back empty. He doesn't laugh. He lowers the stylus slowly, the way a man sets down a cup he's decided not to drink from.

"Twenty sacks," he says, flat. "To a bakery I haven't got, on a sheet I never nailed up. And you've been there and back in the time it took Wim to water his horse." He taps the tablet once, hard. "Friend, either the sun's cooked you, or you've worked this patter in other towns. I'm not paying out a tenth of nothing, and I'm not writing your mark down against it."

Then he squints. "Ledger, though. You said ledger."

He jerks his chin at the barrel cart. Its driver has climbed down, a lean, freckled woman with ink-stained fingers. She's walking slowly around her cart and lifting every tarp as if the thing might be hiding under one.

"Bettany. Lost her tally book off the back somewhere on the north road this morning. Every debt she's owed is in it, and she's asked half the square already." His eyes come back to you, cooler than before. "If you've *really* seen it, tell her where. If you haven't, don't you dare tell her you have."

Bettany looks up, having heard her name.

result.summary: 5 minutes pass (Short, sour exchange with Tobin at the square)

narration:
"Again," Tobin says.

He doesn't raise his voice. He doesn't have to. The square is small, and the man watering his horse at the trough has stopped pretending not to listen.

"There's no *again*, friend. There was no *first*." He lets the wax tablet drop back on its cord and folds his arms over it. "No sheet, no sacks, no bakery, no coin. I've said it plain twice now. I'll not say it a fourth time."

Bettany has come halfway across the square, with one tarp still bunched in her fist. She looks from Tobin to you and rubs her ink-stained fingers together. "This the one who saw my book?"

"This is the one who *says* things," Tobin answers, and the man at the trough snorts.

Bettany's face closes like a ledger snapping shut. "Right." She turns back toward her cart, counting under her breath, though not about you. You catch names and sums: *Corran, four. The Millwards, six and a half.* Debts she can't prove without the book.

Tobin nods toward the road out of the square. "North road's that way, if you want to *find* something instead of telling me you have. Granary's past the well, if you want honest coin by sundown. Ford's south." He turns his back on you to scrape a smudge off the tablet. "Pick one and do it. Folk here remember faces."

At the trough, the horse-waterer swings up onto his wagon. By the look on his face, he's already telling it in his head.
